claim: Normal mouse chow contains phytochemicals that can act as precursors of AhR agonists, in particular indole-3-carbinole (I3C).
source: Normal mouse chow contains phytochemicals that can act as precursors of AhR agonists, in particular indole-3-carbinole (I3C) (Bjeldanes et al., 1991), which is detected in the serum of mice fed on normal chow diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bjeldanes et al., 1991 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing detection in serum

claim: I3C is detected in the serum of mice fed on normal chow diet.
source: Normal mouse chow contains phytochemicals that can act as precursors of AhR agonists, in particular indole-3-carbinole (I3C) (Bjeldanes et al., 1991), which is detected in the serum of mice fed on normal chow diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: I3C concentration in the serum of mice fed on the AhR-poor or I3C diet was significantly different.
source: As a proof of principle, we verified that I3C concentration in the serum of mice fed on the AhR-poor or I3C diet was significantly different (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Mice fed on the normal chow and I3C diets showed similar expression of Cyp1a1.
source: Mice fed on the normal chow and I3C diets showed similar expression of Cyp1a1, while mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had almost undetectable expression of Cyp1a1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had almost undetectable expression of Cyp1a1.
source: Mice fed on the normal chow and I3C diets showed similar expression of Cyp1a1, while mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had almost undetectable expression of Cyp1a1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: The AhR-poor diet contains negligeable amounts of natural AhR agonists.
source: Mice fed on the normal chow and I3C diets showed similar expression of Cyp1a1, while mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had almost undetectable expression of Cyp1a1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), validating that the AhR-poor diet contains negligeable amounts of natural AhR agonists.
evidence: Inferred from the undetectable expression of Cyp1a1 in mice fed on AhR-poor diet, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: After footpad injection of papain, similar Th2 induction was observed in the draining lymph nodes in mice fed on normal chow or I3C diet.
source: After footpad injection of papain, we observed similar Th2 induction in the draining lymph nodes in both groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: IL4 and IL13 were increased by papain exposure.
source: IL4 and IL13 were increased by papain exposure, while IL5 secretion was not significantly different from the control condition.
evidence: Stated as observation from experimental data

claim: IL5 secretion was not significantly different from the control condition after papain exposure.
source: IL4 and IL13 were increased by papain exposure, while IL5 secretion was not significantly different from the control condition.
evidence: Stated as observation from experimental data

claim: DIM, but not L-kynurenin or indole-3-acetic acid, was decreased in the serum of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet.
source: DIM, but not L-kynurenin or indole-3-acetic acid, was decreased in the serum of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Epidermal hyperplasia upon papain exposure occurred only in the foot of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet.
source: Histological analysis showed epidermal hyperplasia upon papain exposure only in the foot of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A, 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: The number of CD4 T cells and B cells was similar in mice fed on the I3C or AhR-poor diets after papain footpad injection.
source: The number of CD4 T cells and B cells was similar in mice fed on the IC3 or AhR-poor diets (Figure 1C), suggesting that the diet had no impact on CD4 T cells or B cells proliferation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The diet had no impact on CD4 T cells or B cells proliferation.
source: The number of CD4 T cells and B cells was similar in mice fed on the IC3 or AhR-poor diets (Figure 1C), suggesting that the diet had no impact on CD4 T cells or B cells proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from the similar numbers of CD4 T cells and B cells shown in Figure 1C

claim: IL4 secretion was induced similarly in both diet groups after papain footpad injection.
source: While IL4 secretion was induced similarly in both groups of mice, the production by T cells of Th2 cytokines IL5 and IL13 was exacerbated in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The production by T cells of Th2 cytokines IL5 and IL13 was exacerbated in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet after papain footpad injection.
source: While IL4 secretion was induced similarly in both groups of mice, the production by T cells of Th2 cytokines IL5 and IL13 was exacerbated in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Mice fed on the AhR-poor diet showed higher secretion of IL5 and IL13 upon papain topical application.
source: Similarly, we found that mice fed on the AhR-poor diet showed higher secretion of IL5 and IL13 upon papain exposure.
evidence: Stated as observation from experimental data in the epicutaneous sensitization model

claim: The secretion of IL10, IFN-γ, and IL17A upon papain challenge was increased in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet in the footpad setting.
source: The secretion of IL10, IFN-γ, and IL17A upon papain challenge was also increased in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet in the footpad setting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), but not with topical application (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: The secretion of IL10, IFN-γ, and IL17A upon papain challenge was not increased in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet with topical application.
source: The secretion of IL10, IFN-γ, and IL17A upon papain challenge was also increased in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet in the footpad setting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), but not with topical application (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: Lack of dietary AhR ligands amplifies allergic responses after cutaneous allergen exposure.
source: We concluded that lack of dietary AhR ligands amplifies allergic responses after cutaneous allergen exposure.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations showing increased Th2 responses in mice fed on AhR-poor diet

claim: There was no difference in cell numbers in the bronchoalveolar space between mice fed on the I3C or AhR-poor diets after intranasal papain exposure.
source: Papain challenge induced airway inflammation with infiltration of eosinophils, monocytes, and CD4 T cells as assessed in the bronchoalveolar space (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1). There was no difference in cell numbers between mice fed on the I3C or AhR-poor diets (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: IL13 and IL5 cytokine secretion in the bronchoalveolar lavage was not increased by the AhR-poor diet compared to I3C diet after intranasal papain exposure.
source: We could also detect IL13 and IL5 in the bronchoalveolar lavage, but cytokine secretion was not increased by the AhR-poor diet compared to I3C diet (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The production of Th2 cytokines by T cells from the pulmonary lymph nodes was similar between diets after intranasal papain exposure.
source: The production of Th2 cytokines by T cells from the pulmonary lymph nodes was also similar between diets (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Papain challenge increased the expression of Muc5ac and Gob5 in the lungs to a similar extent in mice fed on I3C or AhR-poor diets.
source: Papain challenge increased the expression of Muc5ac and Gob5 in the lungs, to a similar extent in mice fed on I3C or AhR-poor diets (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: IgE concentration in the blood was comparable in both diet groups of papain-exposed mice after intranasal exposure.
source: Finally, we measured the concentration of IgE in the blood and found comparable levels in both groups of papain-exposed mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The lack of dietary AhR ligands does not affect airway type 2 allergic responses.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the lack of dietary AhR ligands does not affect airway type 2 allergic responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations showing no difference in airway allergy parameters between diets

claim: Cutaneous allergen exposure can lead to airway allergy to the same allergen via the induction of Th2 memory CD4 T cells by skin DC.
source: Cutaneous allergen exposure can lead to airway allergy to the same allergen via the induction of Th2 memory CD4 T cells by skin DC (Deckers et al., 2017a), a phenomenon referred to as 'atopic march' (Bantz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deckers et al., 2017a and Bantz et al., 2014

claim: Lack of dietary AhR ligands during the sensitization phase increased the infiltration in the bronchoalveolar space of eosinophils, monocytes, and CD4 T cells after skin sensitization followed by intranasal papain exposure.
source: While the number of alveolar macrophages was unaffected by the diet, lack of dietary AhR ligands during the sensitization phase increased the infiltration in the bronchoalveolar space of eosinophils, monocytes, and CD4 T cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: IL13 secretion was higher in the bronchoalveolar lavage of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet during the sensitization phase.
source: IL13 secretion was higher in the bronchoalveolar lavage of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet during the sensitization phase, and IL5 concentration showed an increased tendency that was not statistically significant (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: IL5 concentration in the bronchoalveolar lavage showed an increased tendency that was not statistically significant in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet during the sensitization phase.
source: IL13 secretion was higher in the bronchoalveolar lavage of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet during the sensitization phase, and IL5 concentration showed an increased tendency that was not statistically significant (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The expression of Muc5ac and Gob5 in lung tissues was significantly increased in mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands during the sensitization phase.
source: Finally, the expression of Muc5ac and of Gob5 in lung tissues was significantly increased in mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands during the sensitization phase (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The lack of dietary AhR ligands during cutaneous allergen exposure worsens subsequent airway allergy.
source: These results show that the lack of dietary AhR ligands during cutaneous allergen exposure worsens subsequent airway allergy.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations in the atopic march model

claim: AhR is expressed by Langerhans cells.
source: AhR is expressed by Langerhans cells and has been proposed to regulate their numbers in the epidermis (Hong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2020

claim: AhR has been proposed to regulate Langerhans cells numbers in the epidermis.
source: AhR is expressed by Langerhans cells and has been proposed to regulate their numbers in the epidermis (Hong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2020

claim: There was no significant difference between diets in Langerhans cells density in the epidermis.
source: We first imaged the epidermis of mice expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP) under the promoter of Cd207/Langerin gene (Kissenpfennig et al., 2005; Figure 4A). We found no significant difference between diets in Langerhans cells density.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A

claim: There was no significant difference between diets in Langerhans cells numbers in the footpad epidermis by flow cytometry.
source: To confirm this observation using another approach, we analyzed footpad epidermal cells by flow cytometry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and found no significant difference between diets in Langerhans cells numbers.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Langerhans cells numbers in the lymph nodes were significantly lower upon papain exposure in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet.
source: Langerhans cells numbers in the lymph nodes were significantly lower upon papain exposure in mice fed on the AhR-poor diet (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Papain exposure increased the number of migratory skin cDC1 and cDC2 independently of the diet.
source: By contrast, papain exposure increased the number of migratory skin cDC1 and cDC2 independently of the diet (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Migratory PDL2+ cDC2 play an essential role in the induction of allergic Th2 responses.
source: In particular, migratory PDL2+ cDC2 play an essential role in the induction of allergic Th2 responses (Gao et al., 2013; Kumamoto et al., 2013), and their number was similar in papain-treated mice from both diet groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gao et al., 2013 and Kumamoto et al., 2013

claim: The number of migratory PDL2+ cDC2 was similar in papain-treated mice from both diet groups.
source: In particular, migratory PDL2+ cDC2 play an essential role in the induction of allergic Th2 responses (Gao et al., 2013; Kumamoto et al., 2013), and their number was similar in papain-treated mice from both diet groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The number of lymph node resident DC was similar in both diet groups.
source: In addition, the number of lymph node resident DC was similar in both diet groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The expression of MHC class II molecules or co-stimulatory molecule CD40 was not affected by the diet.
source: The expression of MHC class II molecules or co-stimulatory molecule CD40 was not affected by the diet (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Langerhans cells number was significantly reduced in papain-treated mice fed on the AhR-poor diet after topical application.
source: The numbers of resident and migratory cDC1 and cDC2 were increased in both diet groups upon papain exposure compared to vehicle treatment, while Langerhans cells number was significantly reduced in papain-treated mice fed on the AhR-poor diet.
evidence: Stated as observation from experimental data in the epicutaneous sensitization model

claim: Lack of dietary AhR ligands impairs Langerhans cells migration upon papain challenge.
source: Collectively, our results show that lack of dietary AhR ligands impairs Langerhans cells migration upon papain challenge.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations showing reduced Langerhans cells in lymph nodes

claim: Langerhans cells migration was significantly reduced in mice treated with the AhR inhibitor CH-223191.
source: Langerhans cells migration, but not that of cDC1 or cDC2, was significantly reduced in mice treated with the AhR inhibitor (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Migration of cDC1 or cDC2 was not significantly reduced in mice treated with the AhR inhibitor CH-223191.
source: Langerhans cells migration, but not that of cDC1 or cDC2, was significantly reduced in mice treated with the AhR inhibitor (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Impaired Langerhans cells migration in mice fed with the AhR-poor diet is due to reduced AhR activation.
source: This result suggests that impaired Langerhans cells migration in mice fed with the AhR-poor diet is due to reduced AhR activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AhR inhibitor treatment reduced Langerhans cells migration

claim: Langerhans cells play an essential role in dampening T cell responses in skin-draining lymph nodes.
source: Langerhans cells play an essential role in dampening T cell responses in skin-draining lymph nodes (Igyarto et al., 2009; Kaplan et al., 2005; Gomez de Agüero et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Igyarto et al., 2009, Kaplan et al., 2005, and Gomez de Agüero et al., 2012

claim: IL5 and IL13 secretion was significantly increased by Langerhans cells depletion.
source: While IL4 secretion was similar in both groups, IL5 and IL13 secretion was significantly increased by Langerhans cells depletion (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: IL4 secretion was similar in both Langerhans cells depleted and control groups.
source: While IL4 secretion was similar in both groups, IL5 and IL13 secretion was significantly increased by Langerhans cells depletion (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Exacerbated Th2 responses in the absence of dietary AhR ligands are caused by impaired Langerhans cells migration to the lymph nodes.
source: We concluded that exacerbated Th2 responses in the absence of dietary AhR ligands are caused by impaired Langerhans cells migration to the lymph nodes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations showing that Langerhans cells depletion mimics the effects of AhR-poor diet

claim: Papain exposure induced a common transcriptomic program in epidermal cells.
source: Papain exposure induced a common transcriptomic program (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), enriched for type I interferon pathway, cytokine-mediated signaling, matrix remodeling, and oncostatin M pathway (a regulator of keratinocyte activation) (Boniface et al., 2007; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B

claim: The common transcriptomic program induced by papain exposure was enriched for type I interferon pathway, cytokine-mediated signaling, matrix remodeling, and oncostatin M pathway.
source: Papain exposure induced a common transcriptomic program (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), enriched for type I interferon pathway, cytokine-mediated signaling, matrix remodeling, and oncostatin M pathway (a regulator of keratinocyte activation) (Boniface et al., 2007; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Oncostatin M pathway is a regulator of keratinocyte activation.
source: Papain exposure induced a common transcriptomic program (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), enriched for type I interferon pathway, cytokine-mediated signaling, matrix remodeling, and oncostatin M pathway (a regulator of keratinocyte activation) (Boniface et al., 2007; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boniface et al., 2007

claim: Both papain-treated groups had significantly increased expression of inflammatory mediators genes (such as Csf1, Ccl20, and Tslp).
source: Consistent with pathway enrichment results, both papain-treated groups had significantly increased expression of inflammatory mediators genes (such as Csf1, Ccl20, and Tslp), interferon-stimulated genes (including Stat1 and Oasl2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and genes involved in tissue repair and remodeling (such as Areg, Il24, Mmp13, Osmr, Tgfa, and Vegfa) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Both papain-treated groups had significantly increased expression of interferon-stimulated genes (including Stat1 and Oasl2).
source: Consistent with pathway enrichment results, both papain-treated groups had significantly increased expression of inflammatory mediators genes (such as Csf1, Ccl20, and Tslp), interferon-stimulated genes (including Stat1 and Oasl2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and genes involved in tissue repair and remodeling (such as Areg, Il24, Mmp13, Osmr, Tgfa, and Vegfa) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Both papain-treated groups had significantly increased expression of genes involved in tissue repair and remodeling (such as Areg, Il24, Mmp13, Osmr, Tgfa, and Vegfa).
source: Consistent with pathway enrichment results, both papain-treated groups had significantly increased expression of inflammatory mediators genes (such as Csf1, Ccl20, and Tslp), interferon-stimulated genes (including Stat1 and Oasl2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and genes involved in tissue repair and remodeling (such as Areg, Il24, Mmp13, Osmr, Tgfa, and Vegfa) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Differentially expressed genes between diets were overexpressed mostly in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet.
source: Differentially expressed genes between diets were overexpressed mostly in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet (Figure 5A), both in basal conditions and upon papain challenge (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: Diet-modulated genes were enriched for regulation of extracellular matrix, cytokine signaling, and inflammatory responses, including the leptin pathway.
source: Diet-modulated genes were enriched for regulation of extracellular matrix, cytokine signaling, and inflammatory responses, including the leptin pathway (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: Mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had in papain-treated epidermis significantly higher expression of matrix components (such as Col1a1, Col4a1, Col5a1) and cell adhesion molecules (including Itgb2 and Itgb7).
source: Consistent with this, mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had in papain-treated epidermis significantly higher expression of matrix components (such as Col1a1, Col4a1, Col5a1) and cell adhesion molecules (including Itgb2 and Itgb7) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F

claim: Mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had in papain-treated epidermis significantly higher expression of inflammatory genes including cytokine Il1b and chemokines Cxcl1, Cxcl3, Cxcl5, Ccl2, and Ccl3.
source: Consistent with this, mice fed on the AhR-poor diet had in papain-treated epidermis significantly higher expression of matrix components (such as Col1a1, Col4a1, Col5a1) and cell adhesion molecules (including Itgb2 and Itgb7) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), and inflammatory genes including cytokine Il1b (Figure 5D) and chemokines Cxcl1, Cxcl3, Cxcl5, Ccl2, and Ccl3 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D

claim: CCL2, CCL3, and CXCL1 were more released upon papain treatment in the skin of mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands.
source: To confirm these results at the protein level, we analyzed the secretion of chemokines using skin explants. CCL2, CCL3, and CXCL1 were more released upon papain treatment in the skin of mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands (Figure 5E), consistent with mRNA expression.
evidence: Supported by protein measurement data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Homeostatic activation of AhR via dietary ligands down-modulates inflammatory pathways in epidermal cells.
source: Collectively, these results show that homeostatic activation of AhR via dietary ligands down-modulates inflammatory pathways in epidermal cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from transcriptomic and protein data showing increased inflammatory gene expression and chemokine secretion in AhR-poor diet mice

claim: AhR is involved in keratinocyte differentiation and maintenance of skin barrier integrity.
source: AhR is involved in keratinocyte differentiation and maintenance of skin barrier integrity (Haas et al., 2016; van den Bogaard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haas et al., 2016 and van den Bogaard et al., 2015

claim: AhR ligands produced by commensal microbiota have been shown to be essential in keratinocyte differentiation and maintenance of skin barrier integrity.
source: AhR ligands produced by commensal microbiota have been shown to be essential in this process (Uberoi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uberoi et al., 2021

claim: The GO signature for keratinocyte differentiation was enriched in the epidermis of SPF mice.
source: The GO signature for keratinocyte differentiation was enriched in the epidermis of SPF mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), consistent with previous findings that microbiota-derived AhR ligands control the expression of genes involved in barrier function such as Cdsn, Cldn1, Dsc1, Dsg1a, Flg, Ivl, and Tjp3, and of keratine molecules including Krt10 (Uberoi et al., 2021; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: Microbiota-derived AhR ligands control the expression of genes involved in barrier function such as Cdsn, Cldn1, Dsc1, Dsg1a, Flg, Ivl, and Tjp3, and of keratine molecules including Krt10.
source: The GO signature for keratinocyte differentiation was enriched in the epidermis of SPF mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), consistent with previous findings that microbiota-derived AhR ligands control the expression of genes involved in barrier function such as Cdsn, Cldn1, Dsc1, Dsg1a, Flg, Ivl, and Tjp3, and of keratine molecules including Krt10 (Uberoi et al., 2021; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uberoi et al., 2021 and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: The genes overexpressed in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet were not enriched in SPF versus germ-free mice.
source: By contrast, the genes overexpressed in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet were not enriched in any group (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: The expression of chemokine genes or Itgb8 was comparable between SPF and germ-free mice.
source: In particular, the expression of chemokine genes or Itgb8 was comparable between SPF and germ-free mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: Lack of dietary AhR ligands had no impact on, or even increased, the expression of keratinocyte barrier genes.
source: In addition, we found that lack of dietary AhR ligands had no impact on, or even increased, the expression of keratinocyte barrier genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: No diet-dependent defect in stratum corneum was observed by histology.
source: Consistent with this, we did not observe by histology any diet-dependent defect in stratum corneum, the outer layer of epidermis formed by cornified keratinocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A

claim: The ultra-structure of the epidermis was similar in both diet groups.
source: In addition, the ultra-structure of the epidermis was similar in both diet groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B

claim: The epidermal barrier function was not compromised in mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands.
source: These observations suggest that the epidermal barrier function was not compromised in mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands and that diet-derived AhR ligands do not impact keratinocyte barrier.
evidence: Inferred from observations showing no defects in stratum corneum structure or barrier gene expression

claim: Diet-derived AhR ligands do not impact keratinocyte barrier.
source: These observations suggest that the epidermal barrier function was not compromised in mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands and that diet-derived AhR ligands do not impact keratinocyte barrier.
evidence: Inferred from observations showing no defects in stratum corneum structure or barrier gene expression

claim: Langerhans cells migration is regulated by Tgf-β, which retains Langerhans cells in the epidermis.
source: Langerhans cells migration is regulated by Tgf-β, which retains Langerhans cells in the epidermis (Kel et al., 2010; Bobr et al., 2012; Mohammed et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kel et al., 2010, Bobr et al., 2012, and Mohammed et al., 2016

claim: Bioactive Tgf-β can be produced from the latent form upon cleavage by integrin-β8 expressed on keratinocytes.
source: Bioactive Tgf-β can be produced from the latent form upon cleavage by integrin-β8 expressed on keratinocytes (Mohammed et al., 2016; Cambier et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2016 and Cambier et al., 2005

claim: One of the pathways enriched in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet was related to Tgf-β regulation.
source: One of the pathways enriched in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet was related to Tgf-β regulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Expression of Itgb8 was significantly higher in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet, with or without papain treatment.
source: Indeed, expression of Itgb8 was significantly higher in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet, with or without papain treatment (Figure 6A), suggesting increased release of bioactive Tgf-β in the skin of mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Increased expression of Itgb8 suggests increased release of bioactive Tgf-β in the skin of mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands.
source: Indeed, expression of Itgb8 was significantly higher in the epidermis of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet, with or without papain treatment (Figure 6A), suggesting increased release of bioactive Tgf-β in the skin of mice deprived of dietary AhR ligands.
evidence: Inferred from the higher expression of Itgb8, which cleaves latent TGF-β to produce bioactive form

claim: The concentration of bioactive Tgf-β, but not that of total Tgf-β, was significantly higher in the skin of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet.
source: To directly test this, we measured total and bioactive Tgf-β release in skin explants. The concentration of bioactive Tgf-β, but not that of total Tgf-β, was significantly higher in the skin of mice fed on the AhR-poor diet (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by protein measurement data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Canonical AhR target genes were upregulated in the FICZ-treated human skin samples.
source: As expected, canonical AhR target genes were upregulated in the FICZ-treated samples (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of public transcriptomic data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Chemokine genes (CCL2, CCL3, CXCL1, CXCL3, CXCL5) and ITGB8 were more expressed in SR1-treated human skin.
source: By contrast, chemokine genes (CCL2, CCL3, CXCL1, CXCL3, CXCL5) and ITGB8 were more expressed in SR1-treated skin (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of public transcriptomic data shown in Figure 6C

claim: AhR activation increased the expression of canonical target genes CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 in human keratinocytes.
source: AhR activation increased the expression of canonical target genes CYP1A1 and CYP1B1, but decreased the expression of ITGB8 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from HaCaT cells shown in Figure 6D

claim: AhR activation decreased the expression of ITGB8 in human keratinocytes.
source: AhR activation increased the expression of canonical target genes CYP1A1 and CYP1B1, but decreased the expression of ITGB8 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from HaCaT cells shown in Figure 6D

claim: Total Tgf-β concentration was similar between AhR agonist and antagonist treatments in human keratinocytes.
